title: Two dimensional inhomogeneous classical systems at criticality
abstract: We study simple inhomogeneous deformations of known two-dimensional classical lattice models described by conformal field theory (CFT) at large distances. The deformations are chosen to vary slowly at lattice scales, while preserving critical behavior. Globally, we find that such systems are described by a CFT in curved space, and identify the underlying space metric. Our two examples are the Ising model and the six vertex model with domain wall boundary conditions. In the latter boundaries are also inhomogeneous, which complicates the analysis. We nevertheless solve the free case using hydrodynamics. In the presence of interactions we determine the arctic curve which separates a critical fluctuating region from an ordered (frozen) phase.
summary: This paper analyzes two-dimensional classical lattice models at criticality when subjected to slow spatial variations. It demonstrates that these inhomogeneous systems are governed by Conformal Field Theory defined on a curved space, successfully deriving the underlying metric for both the Ising and six vertex models. This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework connecting lattice statistics, CFT, and geometry.
main_problem: The study investigates how critical behavior of two-dimensional classical lattice models is modified by slow, spatially varying (inhomogeneous) deformations.
main_result: Such inhomogeneous systems are shown to be described by a Conformal Field Theory formulated on a curved space, allowing the identification of the underlying space metric.
method: The analysis combines techniques from Conformal Field Theory (CFT), free fermion mapping via Jordan-Wigner transformation, and hydrodynamic approaches for specific cases.
model_or_system: The primary models are 2D classical lattice systems, specifically the Ising model and the six vertex model with domain wall boundary conditions. The Hamiltonian is defined by local coupling constants that vary slowly across the lattice.
key_observables: Spin correlation functions, the energy gap ($\Delta E$), and the 'arctic curve' separating critical fluctuating regions from ordered phases.
important_parameters: Coupling constants ($K, K'$), the deformation function $f(x/N)$, and the system size $N$ (in the large $N$ limit).
main_assumptions: The deformations are assumed to vary slowly at lattice scales while crucially preserving the underlying critical behavior.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagram of the Ising model, show the structure of the inhomogeneous lattice couplings, and provide numerical comparisons between calculated gaps/correlations and CFT predictions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general framework using CFT for slow deformations to applying this formalism specifically to the 2D Ising model, deriving the curved space metric, and finally solving specific cases like the six vertex model using hydrodynamics.
why_interesting: The connection between lattice statistical mechanics models (like the Ising model) and continuum field theories in curved spacetime provides a powerful tool for understanding how geometry influences critical phenomena, which is relevant to effective Hamiltonians in AMO physics.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Phase diagram of the two-dimensional Ising model. The critical line (4) shown in blue separates an ordered phase from a disordered phase. Recall temper- ature is implicit in this diagram, since K = βJ and K′ = βJ′. All Ising models with parameters on the blue critical line renormalize to the same Ising conformal field theory, so it is not a line of critical points in the field-theoretical sense.

Figure 5: Equal imaginary time spin-spin correlations for N = 256 spins, with notation σ(x) = σ(x, y = 0). Left: homogeneous case with known chord length scaling (11). Right: inhomogeneous case, with deformation f (u) = 1 + a sin2πpu + b sin6πpu, a = 0.7, b = 0.5. Data for p = 1 and p = 2 is shown, and it compares extremely well with the curved spacetime CFT result (23). .

Figure 6: Top figure: representation of the six allowed vertices a1, a2, b1, b2, c1, c2 of the model. The paths can be seen as particle trajectories which can only go to the right, or upwards. They can meet at a given vertex but cannot cross. We also consider a case where vertex weights are particle-hole symmetric, as shown. Bottom figure: color code used in several of the following figures to represent vertex configurations.
